questions.stem:
[In this question, position vectors are given relative to a fixed origin.]
At time $t$ seconds, where $t>0$, a particle $P$ has velocity $\mathbf{v}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ where
$$\mathbf{v} = 3t^2\mathbf{i} - 6t^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{j}$$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the speed of $P$ at time $t = 2$ seconds.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: Put $t=2$ in $\mathbf{v}$ and use Pythagoras: $\sqrt{12^2+(-6\sqrt{2})^2}$
A1: $\sqrt{216}, 6\sqrt{6}$ or 15 or better ($\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find an expression, in terms of $t$, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$, for the acceleration of $P$ at time $t$ seconds, where $t > 0$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Differentiate $\mathbf{v}$ wrt $t$ to obtain $\mathbf{a}$
A1: $6t\mathbf{i} - 3t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{j}$ oe ($\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$) isw

parts.label: c
parts.text:
At time $t = 4$ seconds, the position vector of $P$ is $(\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$.
(c) Find the position vector of $P$ at time $t = 1$ second.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: Integrate $\mathbf{v}$ wrt $t$ to obtain $\mathbf{r}$
A1: $\mathbf{r} = t^3\mathbf{i} - 4t^{\frac{3}{2}}\mathbf{j}\;(+\mathbf{C})$
M1: $(\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j}) = 4^3\mathbf{i} - 4\times 4^{\frac{3}{2}}\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}$
A1: $(-62\mathbf{i}+24\mathbf{j})$ (m) isw e.g. if they go on to find the distance.
Notes: Accept column vectors throughout apart from the answer to (b). 1a M1: Need square root but -ve sign not required. Allow i's and/or j's to go missing from their v at t=2, provided they have applied Pythagoras correctly. A1: cao. N.B. Correct answer with no working can score 2 marks. 1b M1: Both powers decreasing by 1. Allow a column vector. M0 if i or j is missing but allow recovery in (b). A1: cao. Do not accept a column vector. 1c M1: Both powers increasing by 1. M0 if i or j is missing but allow recovery. A1: (r=) not required. M1: Putting r = (i-4j) and t=4 into their displacement vector expression which must have C (allow C) to give an equation in C only, seen or implied. Must have attempted to integrate v for this mark to be available. N.B. C does not need to be found and this is a method mark, so allow slips. A1: cao

questions.stem:
Figure 1
A rough plane is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $\alpha$, where $\tan\alpha = \frac{3}{4}$
A small block $B$ of mass 5 kg is held in equilibrium on the plane by a horizontal force of magnitude $X$ newtons, as shown in Figure 1.
The force acts in a vertical plane which contains a line of greatest slope of the inclined plane.
The block $B$ is modelled as a particle.
The magnitude of the normal reaction of the plane on $B$ is 68.6 N.
Using the model,

parts.label: a(i)
parts.text:
(a) (i) find the magnitude of the frictional force acting on $B$,
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a)(i) M1: Resolve vertically
A1: $F$ acting UP the plane: $(\uparrow)\, F\sin\alpha + 68.6\cos\alpha = 5g$ OR $F$ acting DOWN the plane: $-F\sin\alpha+68.6\cos\alpha=5g$
Other possible equations from which $X$ would need to be eliminated to give an equation in $F$ only to earn the M mark: $(\nwarrow)\,68.6 = X\sin\alpha+5g\cos\alpha$ (leads to $X=49$ with $g=9.8$); $F$ up: $(\nearrow)\,F+X\cos\alpha=5g\sin\alpha$ OR down: $-F+X\cos\alpha=5g\sin\alpha$; $(\rightarrow)\,F\cos\alpha+X=68.6\sin\alpha$ OR $-F\cos\alpha+X=68.6\sin\alpha$
A1: 9.8 (N) (49/5 is A0). N.B. If sin and cos are interchanged in all equations, this leads to an answer of 9.8 in the wrong direction and can only score (a)(i) M1A1A0 (ii) A0.
Notes: 2a(i) M1: Complete method to obtain an equation in F only. For each equation used, correct no. of terms, dimensionally correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved. A1: Correct equation in F only, trig does not need to be substituted. A1: cao (must be positive)

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) state the direction of the frictional force acting on $B$.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (a)(ii) A1: Down the plane (Allow down or downwards or an arrow, but must appear as the answer to (a)(ii) not just on the diagram). cao. Note that this mark is dependent on an answer of 9.8 or -9.8 for (a)(i) from a fully correct solution unless they have used $g=9.81$, in which case the answer will be 9.7 or -9.7 (2sf) see SC2 below. N.B. Allow this mark, if their answer to (a)(i) is fully correct apart from a small error due to use of inaccurate trig i.e using an angle $36.9°$. SC1: If they use $\mu R$ at any point (with an unknown $\mu$) for F in part (a), can score (a)(i) max M1A1A0; (a)(ii) A1, where they must have obtained $\mu R = 9.8$ or $-9.8$, from correct working. SC2: If $g=9.81$ is used consistently throughout 2(a), (leading to $X=48.9…$ and $F=9.7$ (2sf)) can score max (a)(i) M1A1A0 (a)(ii) A1

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The horizontal force of magnitude $X$ newtons is now removed and $B$ moves down the plane.
Given that the coefficient of friction between $B$ and the plane is 0.5
(b) find the acceleration of $B$ down the plane.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) N.B. If they use R=68.6 in this part, the maximum they can score is M1A1M0A0M0A0. If they use F=9.8 or their F from (a) in this part, the maximum they can score is M1A1M0A0M0A0.
M1: Equation of motion down the plane
A1: $5g\sin\alpha - F = 5a$ Allow $(-a)$ instead of $a$
M1: Resolve perpendicular to the plane
A1: $R = 5g\cos\alpha$
M1: $F = 0.5R$ seen
A1: $a = 1.96$ or $2.0$ or $2\,(\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}})$ or $\frac{1}{5}g$
Notes: 2b M1: Correct no. of terms, dimensionally correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved. A1: Correct equation for their F. M1: Correct no. of terms, dimensionally correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved (N.B. M0 if R=68.6(N) is used in this equation). A1: Correct equation. M1: Could be seen on a diagram (N.B. M0 if R=68.6(N) is used). A1: Cao. Must be positive.

questions.stem:
[In this question, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are horizontal unit vectors.]
A particle $P$ of mass 4 kg is at rest at the point $A$ on a smooth horizontal plane.
At time $t = 0$, two forces, $\mathbf{F}_1 = (4\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}$ and $\mathbf{F}_2 = (\lambda\mathbf{i}+\mu\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}$, where $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are constants, are applied to $P$
Given that $P$ moves in the direction of the vector $(3\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})$

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: $(4\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})+(\lambda\mathbf{i}+\mu\mathbf{j}) = (4+\lambda)\mathbf{i}+(-1+\mu)\mathbf{j}$
M1: Use ratios to obtain an equation in $\lambda$ and $\mu$ only
A1: $\frac{(4+\lambda)}{(-1+\mu)}=\frac{3}{1}$ or $\frac{\frac{1}{4}(4+\lambda)}{\frac{1}{4}(-1+\mu)}=\frac{3}{1}$
A1*: $\lambda-3\mu+7=0$* Allow $0=\lambda-3\mu+7$ but nothing else.
Notes: 3a M1: Adding the two forces, i's and j's must be collected (or must be a single column vector) seen or implied. M1: Must be using ratios; Ignore an equation e.g. $(4+\lambda)\mathbf{i}+(-1+\mu)\mathbf{j}=3\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}$ if they go on to use ratios. However, if they write $4+\lambda=3$ and $-1+\mu=1$ then $3(-1+\mu)=3$ so $4+\lambda=3(-1+\mu)$ with no use of a constant, it's M0. They may use the acceleration, with a factor of $\frac{1}{4}$ top and bottom, see alternative. Allow one side of the equation to be inverted. A1: Correct equation. A1*: Given answer correctly obtained. Must see at least one line of working, with the LH fraction 'removed'.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
At time $t = 4$ seconds, $P$ passes through the point $B$.
Given that $\lambda = 2$
(b) find the length of $AB$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: $\lambda=2\Rightarrow \mu=3$; Resultant force $=(6\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})$ (N)
M1: $(6\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})=4\mathbf{a}$ OR $|(6\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})|=4a$
DM1: Use of $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{u}t+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $\mathbf{u}=0$, their $\mathbf{a}$ and $t=4$: Or integrate their a twice with u=0 and put t=4: $\mathbf{r}=\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{(6\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})}{4}4^2=(12\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})$
M1: $\sqrt{12^2+4^2}$
ALTERNATIVE 1: DM1: Use of $s=ut+\frac{1}{2}at^2$, u=0, their a and t=4: $s=\frac{1}{2}\times\sqrt{1.5^2+0.5^2}\times4^2$; M1: Use of Pythagoras to find mag of a: $a=\sqrt{1.5^2+0.5^2}$
ALTERNATIVE 2: DM1: $s=\frac{1}{2}\times\left(\frac{\sqrt{6^2+2^2}}{4}\right)\times4^2$; M1: $|(6\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})|=\sqrt{6^2+2^2}$
A1: $\sqrt{160}, 2\sqrt{40}, 4\sqrt{10}$ oe or 13 or better (m)
Notes: Accept column vectors throughout. 3b M1: Adding F1 and F2 to find the resultant force, $\lambda$ and $\mu$ must be substituted. N.B. M0 if they use $\mu=2$ coming from $-1+\mu=1$ in part (a). M1: Use of F=4a Or |F|=4a, where F is their resultant. (including 3i+j). This is an independent mark, so could be earned, for example, if they have subtracted the forces to find the 'resultant'. N.B. M0 if only using F1 or F2. DM1: Dependent on previous M mark for either use of r=ut+½at² with u=0, their a and t=4 to produce a displacement vector, Or: integrate twice, with u=0, their a and t=4 to produce a displacement Vector, Or: use of s=ut+½at² with u=0, their a and t=4 to produce a length. M1: Use of Pythagoras, with square root, to find the magnitude of their displacement vector, a or F (M0 if only using F1 or F2) depending on which method they have used. A1: cao

questions.stem:
Figure 2
A uniform rod $AB$ has mass $M$ and length $2a$
A particle of mass $2M$ is attached to the rod at the point $C$, where $AC = 1.5a$
The rod rests with its end $A$ on rough horizontal ground.
The rod is held in equilibrium at an angle $\theta$ to the ground by a light string that is attached to the end $B$ of the rod.
The string is perpendicular to the rod, as shown in Figure 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Explain why the frictional force acting on the rod at $A$ acts horizontally to the right on the diagram.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (a) B1: The horizontal component of $T$ acts to the left and since the only other horizontal force is friction, it must act to the right oe. Notes: 4a B1: Any equivalent explanation

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The tension in the string is $T$
(b) Show that $T = 2Mg\cos\theta$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Take moments about $A$ or any other complete method to obtain an equation in $T$, $M$ and $\theta$ only. (see possible equations below that they may use)
A1: $T.2a = Mga\cos\theta + 2Mg\times 1.5a\cos\theta$ (A0 if a's missing)
Other possible equations but F and R would need to be eliminated: $(\nwarrow)\,R\cos\theta+T=F\sin\theta+Mg\cos\theta+2Mg\cos\theta$; $(\nearrow)\,R\sin\theta+F\cos\theta=Mg\sin\theta+2Mg\sin\theta$; $(\rightarrow)\,F=T\sin\theta$; M(B), $R.2a\cos\theta=Mga\cos\theta+2Mg\times0.5a\cos\theta+F.2a\sin\theta$; M(G), $Fa\sin\theta+Ta=Ra\cos\theta+2Mg\times0.5a\cos\theta$; M(C), $R\times1.5a\cos\theta=T\times0.5a+Mg\times0.5a\cos\theta+F\times1.5a\sin\theta$
A1*: $T=2Mg\cos\theta$*
Notes: 4b M1: Correct no. of terms, dimensionally correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors. A1: Correct equation, trig does not need to be substituted (Allow: $T.2a=Mga\cos\theta+3Mga\cos\theta$). A1*: Given answer correctly obtained with no wrong working seen. Allow $2Mg\cos\theta=T$ But not $T=2\cos\theta Mg$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Given that $\cos\theta = \frac{3}{5}$
(c) show that the magnitude of the vertical force exerted by the ground on the rod at $A$ is $\frac{57Mg}{25}$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: e.g. Resolve vertically
A1: $(\uparrow)\,R+T\cos\theta=Mg+2Mg$
A1*: $R=\frac{57Mg}{25}$*
Other possible equations but F would need to be eliminated: (as listed in (b))
Notes: 4c M1: For an equation in $R$, $M$, $T$ and $\theta$ only. Correct no. of terms, dimensionally correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved. A1: Correct equation, T and trig do not need to be substituted. A1*: Given answer correctly obtained with no wrong working seen

parts.label: d
parts.text:
The coefficient of friction between the rod and the ground is $\mu$
Given that the rod is in limiting equilibrium,
(d) show that $\mu = \frac{8}{19}$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) M1: Find an equation containing $F$ e.g. Resolve horizontally
A1: $(\rightarrow)\,F=T\sin\theta$
Other possible equations (as listed in (b))
M1: $F=\mu R$ used i.e. both $F$ and $R$ are substituted.
A1*: $\mu=\frac{8}{19}$*
Notes: 4d M1: For any equation with F in it. Correct no. of terms, dimensionally correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved. A1: Correct equation, trig does not need to be substituted. M1: Must be used i.e. M0 if merely quoting it. A1*: Given answer correctly obtained with no wrong working seen

(a) Explain why the frictional force acting on the rod at $A$ acts horizontally to the right on the diagram.
(1)
The tension in the string is $T$
(b) Show that $T = 2Mg\cos\theta$
(3)
Given that $\cos\theta = \frac{3}{5}$
(c) show that the magnitude of the vertical force exerted by the ground on the rod at $A$ is $\frac{57Mg}{25}$
(3)
The coefficient of friction between the rod and the ground is $\mu$
Given that the rod is in limiting equilibrium,
(d) show that $\mu = \frac{8}{19}$
(4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: The horizontal component of $T$ acts to the left and since the only other horizontal force is friction, it must act to the right oe. Notes: 4a B1: Any equivalent explanation
(b) M1: Take moments about $A$ or any other complete method to obtain an equation in $T$, $M$ and $\theta$ only. (see possible equations below that they may use)
A1: $T.2a = Mga\cos\theta + 2Mg\times 1.5a\cos\theta$ (A0 if a's missing)

A1: $(\uparrow)\,R+T\cos\theta=Mg+2Mg$

Notes: 4c M1: For an equation in $R$, $M$, $T$ and $\theta$ only. Figure 3
A golf ball is at rest at the point $A$ on horizontal ground.
The ball is hit and initially moves at an angle $\alpha$ to the ground.
The ball first hits the ground at the point $B$, where $AB = 120\,\mathrm{m}$, as shown in Figure 3.
The motion of the ball is modelled as that of a particle, moving freely under gravity, whose initial speed is $U\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
Using this model,

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: Using horizontal motion
A1: Whole Motion: $U\cos\alpha\times t=120$ OR Half way: $U\cos\alpha\times t=60$
M1: Using vertical motion
A1: $U\sin\alpha\times t-\frac{1}{2}gt^2=0$ OR $0=U\sin\alpha-gt$
DM1: Attempt to solve problem by eliminating $t$
A1*: $U^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha=588$*
N.B. No credit given if they use the given answer from (b).
Notes: 5a Could score 2/6 for any one of the 4 given equations if there is no corresponding second equation or there is an attempt but it's incorrect. M1: Complete method to give equation in $U$, $\alpha$ and $t$ only, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved. A1: Correct equation. M1: as above. A1: Correct equation. DM1: Eliminate $t$, dependent on first and second M1's. A1*: Given answer correctly obtained, with no wrong working seen. Allow $588=U^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha$ but nothing else

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The ball reaches a maximum height of 10 m above the ground.
(b) Show that $U^2 = 1960$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Using vertical motion OR conservation of energy
A1: $0^2=(U\sin\alpha)^2-2g\times10$ OR $\frac{1}{2}mU^2-\frac{1}{2}m(U\cos\alpha)^2=mg\times10$
ALTERNATIVE 1: If $t$ is time to top: use of $10=\frac{1}{2}gt^2$ oe ($t=\frac{10}{7}$) to obtain an equation in $U$ and $\alpha$ only M1; $U\sin\alpha=14$ or $U\cos\alpha=42$ A1
ALTERNATIVE 2: If $t$ is time to top: use of $10=U\sin\alpha\,t-\frac{1}{2}gt^2$ with $t=\frac{60}{U\cos\alpha}$ substituted to obtain an equation in $U$ and $\alpha$ only M1; $10=U\sin\alpha\times\frac{60}{U\cos\alpha}-\frac{1}{2}g\left(\frac{60}{U\cos\alpha}\right)^2$ A1
DM1: Attempt to solve problem by eliminating $\alpha$: e.g. $U\sin\alpha=14\Rightarrow U\cos\alpha=42$, from part (a) or from using $t=\frac{10}{7}$, then square and add to give result OR: $U^2\sin^2\alpha=20g=196$ and $U^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha=588$, divide to give $\tan\alpha=\frac{1}{3}$ then $\sin^2\alpha=\frac{1}{10}$, hence result OR in ALTERNATIVE 2: sub for $U^2$ using part (a), to give $\tan\alpha=\frac{1}{3}$ then $\sin^2\alpha=\frac{1}{10}$, hence result
N.B. Just stating that $\sin^2\alpha=\frac{1}{10}$, with no working is DM0A0.
A1*: $U^2=1960$*
N.B. Verification (i.e. starting with $U^2=1960$ and trying to work backwards) is not an acceptable method for this question.
Notes: 5b M1: Complete method to give equation in $U$ and $\alpha$ only with correct no. of terms, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved. A1: Correct equation. DM1: Eliminate $\alpha$ and rearrange, dependent on first M1. A1*: Given answer correctly obtained with no wrong working seen (N.B. If they use a value for $\alpha$ ($18.43°$) they lose the final A1*)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
In a refinement to the model, the effect of air resistance is included.
The motion of the ball, from $A$ to $B$, is now modelled as that of a particle whose initial speed is $V\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
This refined model is used to calculate a value for $V$
(c) State which is greater, $U$ or $V$, giving a reason for your answer.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (c) B1: $V$, since air resistance has to be overcome, or just 'because of air resistance' isw

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) State one further refinement to the model that would make the model more realistic.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (d) B1: e.g. wind effects, more accurate value of $g$, spin of ball, size of ball, shape of ball, dimensions of ball, not a particle, variable acceleration, surface area of ball, humidity. Allow wind resistance and rotational resistance (Ignore any mention of air resistance or drag). Notes: 5c B1: Clear statement isw. 5d B1: B0 if there is an incorrect extra e.g. mass or weight
